classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the substitution producing alternating powers of 3 in the standard expansion.

content.prompt:
By considering the expansion of $(1+x)^n$, show that
$$\binom{n}{0}-\binom{n}{1}3+\binom{n}{2}3^2-\cdots+(-1)^n\binom{n}{n}3^n=(-2)^n.$$

answer.short: Substitute $x=-3$ into the expansion of $(1+x)^n$; its left-hand side becomes $(1-3)^n=(-2)^n$.
answer.worked:
The binomial theorem gives
$$(1+x)^n=\binom{n}{0}+\binom{n}{1}x+\binom{n}{2}x^2+\cdots+\binom{n}{n}x^n.$$
Substitute $x=-3$:
$$(1-3)^n=\binom{n}{0}+\binom{n}{1}(-3)+\binom{n}{2}(-3)^2+\cdots+\binom{n}{n}(-3)^n.$$
Since $(-3)^k=(-1)^k3^k$,
$$(-2)^n=\binom{n}{0}-\binom{n}{1}3+\binom{n}{2}3^2-\cdots+(-1)^n\binom{n}{n}3^n,$$
which proves the identity.
